newsitem.title: PERU: Peru gov't says meeting with rebels called off.
newsitem.headline: Peru gov't says meeting with rebels called off.

text.p: A long-awaited meeting on Sunday between Peru's chief negotiator and Marxist rebels still holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence was cancelled, dashing hopes of an end to the 26-day crisis.

Education Minister and chief negotiator Domingo Palermo told a news conference the planned meeting was called off after the rebels told him it could only take place if he took with him a proposal to free some 400 jailed members of the Tupac Amaru Revollutionary Movement (MRTA).
"If I did not, it was preferable not to meet, as there was no possibility of talking," Palermo told a news conference. "I really regret this."
This main rebel demand has been repeatedly rejected by Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori.
Palermo said he had sent a written proposal to Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, head of the MRTA rebels in the residence, containing the government's conditions for resuming talks.

These included the establishment of a "guarantor commission" made up of representatives from the government, the MRTA, the Vatican and the International Committee of the Red Cross, who would jointly seek a peaceful end to the standoff.
Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, who has visited the residence regularly throughout the crisis, had been named the Vatican's representative to the commission, Palermo said.

Sunday's scheduled meeting, arranged in a walkie-talkie conversation between Palermo and Cerpa on Friday, would have been their second face-to-face encounter since the rebels stormed a diplomatic reception on Dec. 17, taking more than 500 hostages.
The two men had not met since holding talks inside the residence on Dec. 28. They have since exchanged several written messages.

Palermo said he would no longer be in radio contact with Cerpa, at the request of the rebels, because an unidentified reporter had leaked a tape recording of their Friday conversation. He was still in touch via other means, he said.
The possibility of a face-to-face meeting had fuelled optimism that an end to the stand-off might be at hand.

"I expect direct negotiations this time to be held smoothly and vigorously and bring about a tangible resolution," Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda earlier told NHK television network in Tokyo.
Of the hundreds of hostages it took, the MRTA has released the majority in what it has called "goodwill gestures."
The last major release of 20 hostages coincided with Palermo's first visit to the compound.

While seeking an early resolution to the standoff, Ikeda reiterated Tokyo's concern that the lives of the remaining hostages was paramount. "The most important thing is the safe release of all the hostages. This should take priority over the time element," he said.
The rebels are holding on to the most valuable hostages, including dozens of Peruvian officials and Fujimori's younger brother, as bargaining chips to obtain the release of their jailed comrades.
Fujimori has insisted he will not give in to "terrorist blackmail" and has urged the rebels to lay down their arms and release all the captives.
His government has, however, floated the possibility of granting the rebels political exile abroad if they surrender.

Cipriani returned to the residence for the second time in two days on Sunday and was believed to have held Mass for the captives. The visits of the bishop, a close friend of Fujimori, inside the compound have often been associated with hostage releases.

In another apparent breach of security at the siege site, two photographers -- identified as employees of the Peruvian investigative magazine Caretas -- hoisted themselves onto a garden wall at the rear of the besieged compound and from about 50 yards (meters) took photographs.

Thousands of Peruvians from Lima's shantytowns converged behind the security cordon around the residence and appealed to the guerrillas to free their captives. The protesters voiced strong support for Fujimori's tough line.
"Support for Fujimori. Do not give in to terrorists," the crowd chanted.
